title: Disable assertions for release builds
description:
Currently our build generates very many warnings if
G_DISABLE_ASSERT is defined.

Add ws_assert() and ws_assert_not_reached() to incrementally
replace existing assertions and then disable them using
WS_DISABLE_ASSERT.

Assertions are disabled with CMake build types
Release and MinSizeRel. By default the build type is
RelWithDebInfo so the current behaviour of enabling
assertions by default is preserved.

My only concern with this is growing our build configuration matrix. Because this does need some CI testing, it's easy to unknowingly introduce new warnings, mostly with used/unused variables.

I'm not sure if there is anything better that we can do, but isn't this sort of a CMake anti-pattern?  I thought CMake was there to smooth out the platform differences and supply the appropriate compiler flags.

On Windows, CMake generates 4 different build options in the Visual Studio solutions, Release, MinSizeRel, RelWithDebInfo and Debug with NDEBUG defined for the first 3  and _DEBUG for the latter.  One can choose which of the variants to use at compile time and they can all be built in the same Build dir.  Generally RelwithDebInfo is sufficient when debugging unless you really need to see things that get optimised out (e.g. local variables) when you have to switch to the Debug variant.

NDEBUG on Windows will render asserts inoperative.

I have no idea what happens on other platforms.

Lots of discussions on the merits of each define at the usual places, e.g. SO here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2290509/debug-vs-ndebug/2290616#2290616

So which assertions should be tested even in release builds, and which should be tested only during development?

Are there any compilers that can (always or optionally) warn about parameters marked as unused but that are, in fact, used?  The GCC manual documents the "unused" attribute as meaning that

> This attribute, attached to a variable, means that the variable is meant to be possibly unused. GCC does not produce a warning for this variable.

"Possibly" unused suggests that if it *is* used, that's not a problem and shouldn't result in a warning.

However, I seem to remember *some* compiler warning about the "marked as unused but, in fact, used" case.

It's a Clang warning, Wused-but-marked-unused. Kind of a nuisance, like you said it goes against the semantics of Wunused-parameter, and I tried disabling it in the past but there was some push back.

I thought this warning was enabled with Wextra but for some reason it's not actually triggering anymore with our default settings. Weird.
resolved all threads

> So which assertions should be tested even in release builds, and which should be tested only during development?

Generally test code. A simple definition is code paths whose sole purpose is to catch bugs and programming errors. Those that are not executed during normal usage of the program and have no other purpose.

The reason I left `g_assert_not_reached()` always enabled is that it isn't executed during normal usage and disabling it can generate spurious uninitialized variable warnings.

There are some situations with Warray-bounds where sometimes disabling assertions on array indexes and such can trigger those warnings, those can be a somewhat annoying to handle without using assertions.

Sorry to come too late in the discussion, but I'm not sure to understand the purpose of this change. Many asserts are here to prevent a NULL pointer dereference, out of bounds access or indicate programming errors. Deactivating them without ensuring that there is a fail safe code (if possible, which might not be the case) will lead to crashes or hard to diagnose behaviors which is even worse than having the assert IMHO.

It's an optimization, on the basis that we are shipping a consistent program (one that doesn't break its internal assumptions) and that those failures are caught in pre-release testing. It also forces you to think a bit more how to correctly handle errors hopefully.

Actual practice seems to corroborate the first point, because it is pretty rare in my experience that a bug report will actually have an assertion failure (instead of a crash).

Opinions do vary though on whether they should be enabled for release builds though. I mainly take the view that code should compile cleanly without them.

IMHO we are opening a can of worms as now you can have invalid pointers being used. Assuming that pre release checks will exercise all the code (especially when you can have crafted packets) seems too optimistic, and having a code slightly faster does not seem worth the trouble.

The assertions are just checking for NULL pointers. Seems like a leap to go from that to an invalid pointer can of worms.

Just a note, I didn't actually change `proto_report_dissector_bug()` which is called by `DISSECTOR_ASSERT()` and I don't have any plans to change that. That just throws an exception and I think it is fine as it is.

But this discussion is important so please feel free to contribute.

I'm fine with leaving bounds checking for pre-computed sizes enabled. It's not expensive. We could add a separate assertion for that.

Not sure what is special about the wmem scopes, it seems to be simply checking that the in/out logic is correct.

I'll try to measure the difference. For that I need to replace all or most of the other assertions too.

> I'm fine with leaving bounds checking for pre-computed sizes enabled. It's not expensive. We could add a separate assertion for that.

Done in !3044.

I built both with gcc -O3 and ran `tshark -r $file > /dev/null` on the contents of some folder on my computer.
```
~/captures % ls -R *.pcap* | wc -l
49
~/captures % du -hs .
557M	.
```
Ran three times both configurations one after the other, assertions disabled was consistently faster and the difference averaged ~3.9%.

 /* some declarations */

@@ -65,6 +65,7 @@ set(WSUTIL_PUBLIC_HEADERS
 	type_util.h

+/* ws_assert.h
+ *
+ * Wireshark - Network traffic analyzer
+ * By Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
+ * Copyright 1998 Gerald Combs
+ *
+ * SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
+ */
+
+#ifndef __WS_ASSERT_H__
+#define __WS_ASSERT_H__
+
+#include <ws_attributes.h>
+
+/*
+ * ws_assert() cannot produce side effects, otherwise code will
+ * behave differently because of WS_DISABLE_ASSERT, and probably introduce
+ * some nasty bugs.
+ */
+#ifndef WS_DISABLE_ASSERT
+#define ws_assert(expr) g_assert(expr)
+#else
+#define ws_assert(expr)
+#endif
+
+/*
+ * We don't want to disable ws_assert_not_reached() with WS_DISABLE_ASSERT.
+ * That would blast compiler warnings everywhere for no benefit, not
+ * even a miniscule performance gain.
+ *
+ * Note: If the compiler supports unreachable built-ins (which recent
+ * versions of GCC and MSVC do) there is no warning blast with
+ * g_assert_not_reached() and G_DISABLE_ASSERT. However if that is not
+ * the case then g_assert_not_reached() is simply (void)0 and that
+ * causes the spurious warnings, because the compiler can't tell anymore
+ * that a certain code path is not used. We add the call to g_abort() so
+ * that the function never returns, even with G_DISABLE_ASSERT.
+ */
+static inline
+WS_NORETURN void ws_assert_not_reached(void) {
+    g_assert_not_reached();
+    g_abort();
+};
+
+#endif /* __WS_ASSERT_H__ */

@@ -814,6 +814,15 @@ else() # ! MSVC
 		-DG_DISABLE_DEPRECATED
 		-DG_DISABLE_SINGLE_INCLUDES

Disable assertions for release builds

Currently our build generates very many warnings if
G_DISABLE_ASSERT is defined.

Add ws_assert() and ws_assert_not_reached() to incrementally
replace existing assertions and then disable them using
WS_DISABLE_ASSERT.

Assertions are disabled with CMake build type Release.

behaviour of enabling assertions by default is (for now) preserved.

Add some notes to README.Developer.
